topic: stripping and re-coating a thatched cottage roof in water reed, then forming the ridge

provenance.author: CC (batch EN-3)
provenance.notes: napisane niezaleznie od korpusu PL, nie jest tlumaczeniem; urzadzenie obliczeniowe: wilgotnosciomierz do trzciny i krokwi

base: I am stripping the old thatch from a cottage roof and laying a fresh coat of water reed.
A smaller barn stands behind the cottage, and its straw thatch was renewed only three winters ago.
I keep a moisture meter in the workshop, because reed cut in a wet season never dries evenly.
The rafters look sound, though the ridge has slumped badly along the eastern half of the run.
Should I strip the whole roof down to the battens, or work in courses from the eaves upward?
Strip only what is spent, because sound underthatch left in place saves both time and reed.
A slumped ridge usually means the fixings beneath have rotted rather than the reed itself failing.
Work upward in courses from the eaves, and never begin the ridge until the coat is complete.
Each course must be dressed home hard before the next one is laid above it.
I stripped back to the underthatch and found the eastern rafters damp but not yet soft.
The moisture meter reads twenty-four percent up there and only fifteen along the western slope.
Rain has been driving against that gable for years, and the eaves course sits low there.
Do I let the timber dry first, or can I thatch straight over it now?
Let it dry, because reed laid over damp oak traps the wet against the rafter.
Twenty-four percent will fall within a fortnight if you sheet the roof and leave the gable open.
Meanwhile lift the eaves course on that side with a fillet, so rain sheds clear.
A roof that throws water off its edge will outlast one that merely holds it.
The moisture meter fell to sixteen percent in ten days, and the fillet lifted the eaves.
I have laid four courses of reed and dressed each one home with the leggett.
The straw barn behind the cottage has a much shallower pitch than this roof does.
Should the courses lie at a different angle here, or does the pitch not matter?
Pitch governs everything in thatch, and a shallow roof needs a longer overlap between courses.
On a steep roof like yours the water leaves quickly, so the courses may lie thinner.
Keep the butts even and the angle steady, and the coat will weather at one rate.
Uneven dressing shows up after five winters as hollows that gather moss and then hold water.
The coat is finished and the butts run level from the eaves to the ridge line.
Now I must form the ridge, and I have both sedge and split hazel to hand.
The old ridge was a flush one, but the neighbours all seem to prefer block ridges.
Which holds better on a cottage that stands open to the weather from every side?
A flush ridge sheds better on an exposed site, whatever the fashion in your village.
Block ridges look handsome but catch wind along the cut edge and lift in gales.
Use sedge for the ridge itself, since it bends over the apex without cracking.
Peg it down with split hazel liggers, spaced close enough to hold in hard weather.
I laid a flush ridge in sedge and pegged it with hazel every nine inches.
The whole roof looks even now, though the sedge sits paler than the reed beneath.
Winter comes in a month and the cottage stands on a very windy rise.
Is there anything worth doing before the gales, or should I simply leave it alone?
Leave it alone, but walk round the eaves after the first hard blow of winter.
New reed settles in its first season, and a peg or two always works loose.
Netting is worth fitting only if gulls or crows start pulling at the ridge sedge.
By the second spring the coat will have bedded down and need nothing for years.
